title: LLM basics for backend engineers
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Tokens and context windows, sampling, structured output and tool calling, hallucination controls, prompt design, streaming over SSE and caching LLM calls.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: Which statement about tokens and the context window is correct?

options.text: Input and output tokens share the window, so a long prompt leaves less room for the reply.
options.why: Right: prompt plus completion must fit, and providers bill both (output usually costs more per token).

options.text: The window caps only the reply, so any prompt length is fine as long as the answer is short.
options.why: The limit covers the prompt as well as the generated output.

options.text: One token is always exactly one English word, so word counts give exact billing numbers.
options.why: Tokens are sub-word pieces; words, punctuation and code split differently.

options.text: The window is shared across all of a user's past chats, which is how the model remembers them.
options.why: Each request starts fresh; any memory is just text you resend.

questions.explanation: Cost and latency both grow with tokens, which is why history trimming, summarisation and short prompts matter. Interview takeaway: budget input and output tokens per request.

questions.prompt: A bot extracts order numbers from customer emails and should behave as repeatably as possible. Which sampling setting fits best?

options.text: A low temperature close to 0, so the most probable tokens dominate the output.
options.why: Right: low temperature reduces randomness, which suits extraction and classification.

options.text: A high temperature around 1.5, so the bot explores alternative readings of each email.
options.why: High temperature adds variety, the opposite of what extraction needs.

options.text: Temperature 1 with top-p set to 1, since the full distribution is the most faithful one.
options.why: That keeps maximum randomness and makes outputs less repeatable.

options.text: Any temperature, because it changes only latency and has no effect on which tokens are chosen.
options.why: Temperature rescales token probabilities before sampling; it changes content, not speed.

questions.explanation: Low temperature (or a small top-p) suits deterministic tasks; higher values suit brainstorming. Note that even temperature 0 is not a hard guarantee of identical outputs across calls or model updates, so still validate.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which practices keep prompts maintainable in a production LLM service?

options.text: Store system prompts in version control or a registry with an id, and log that id with each request.
options.why: Right: you can tie a bad answer to the exact prompt version.

options.text: Include a few short few-shot examples that cover the tricky edge cases of the task.
options.why: Right: examples show the expected format and edge-case handling better than prose alone.

options.text: Run the golden-dataset evals before a prompt change is rolled out, like a regression test.
options.why: Right: prompt edits can silently break other cases.

options.text: Edit the live prompt in a admin console without history, so fixes ship instantly.
options.why: No history means no rollback and no way to explain a regression.

options.text: Paste user text straight into the instruction block so the model cannot tell them apart.
options.why: Mixing untrusted input into instructions invites prompt injection; delimit and label it.

questions.explanation: Treat prompts like code: versioned, reviewed, tested and traceable. Keep user input clearly separated from instructions.

questions.prompt: A service asks the model for JSON matching a Pydantic model, but occasionally a field is missing or has the wrong type. What is the robust approach?

options.text: Validate with Pydantic; on failure retry with the error message, up to a small limit.
options.why: Right: validation catches the fault and feedback usually fixes it; the cap bounds cost.

options.text: Trust the output, since the prompt already says to reply with valid JSON that follows the schema.
options.why: Prompts reduce but never eliminate malformed output; unvalidated data reaches your logic.

options.text: Strip the text with a regular expression and fill any missing fields with default values silently.
options.why: Silent defaults hide real extraction failures and corrupt downstream data.

options.text: Retry indefinitely at a higher temperature until a response happens to pass validation.
options.why: Unbounded retries burn tokens, and extra randomness makes valid output less likely.

questions.explanation: Use provider-native structured output or tool schemas where available, then still validate server-side. Bounded validate-and-retry is the standard pattern.

questions.prompt: With function (tool) calling for your own custom functions, the model executes the function itself and returns the function result to your application.

options.text: True
options.why: The model only emits a structured request (tool name plus JSON arguments).

options.text: False
options.why: Right: your application runs the function and sends the result back as a message.

questions.explanation: The model proposes a call; your code validates the arguments, executes, and returns the result. That boundary is where you add authorisation and safety checks.

questions.prompt: A policy Q&A bot invents refund rules that are not in the company documents. Which control best addresses the cause?

options.text: Retrieve the policy, answer only from it with citations, and allow "I do not know".
options.why: Right: grounding, citations and abstention attack unsupported answers directly.

options.text: Add the sentence "never hallucinate" to the system prompt and rely on it to keep answers accurate.
options.why: An instruction alone does not give the model facts it lacks.

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores more answers and picks the best-sounding of them.
options.why: More randomness tends to increase unsupported content, not reduce it.

options.text: Switch to a bigger model, because larger models do not produce unsupported statements any more.
options.why: Larger models still hallucinate; they just do it less often on average.

questions.explanation: Hallucinations come from gaps in knowledge and training that rewards fluent guesses. Ground the answer in retrieved sources, require citations you can check, and let the system abstain.

questions.prompt: You want tokens to appear progressively in a browser chat UI from a FastAPI backend. Which design fits?

options.text: An async generator yielding server-sent events in a streaming response.
options.why: Right: SSE over a long-lived HTTP response suits one-way token streams.

options.text: Wait for the full completion, return one JSON body, and let the browser fake a typing effect.
options.why: That keeps time to first token high; the user waits for the whole generation.

options.text: Have the browser poll a status endpoint every second and download the full text each time.
options.why: Polling adds latency and load and resends text that has not changed.

options.text: Open a raw TCP socket from the browser to the model provider with the API key in the page.
options.why: Browsers cannot do this safely, and it would expose your provider key.

questions.explanation: Streaming improves perceived latency (time to first token). Remember to handle client disconnects, cancel the upstream call, and send a final done or error event.

questions.prompt: A semantic cache can return a stored answer for a differently worded but similar question, so a threshold that is too loose risks serving a wrong answer.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: similarity does not mean same intent, so tune the threshold and scope keys such as tenant and model.

options.text: False
options.why: Semantic matching is approximate by design, so a loose threshold can match different questions.

questions.explanation: Exact caches (hash of model, prompt and parameters) are safe but hit rarely; semantic caches hit more but need thresholds, per-tenant isolation and expiry. Prompt caching at the provider is separate: it discounts a repeated prompt prefix.
